title: NVDA Stock Rebounds 4% but $180 Support Remains Critical After Midterm Selloff for Nvidia - FXLeaders
content: Nvidia shares extended their decline from record highs above $243, falling towards $181 before recovering 4% on Friday, as Democratic midterm victories, rising infrastructure costs, electricity constraints and growing opposition to data-centre expansion intensified concerns about the semiconductor industry’s growth prospects. Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) shares dropped below $200 on Thursday, falling towards $181 and extending their retreat from record highs above $243. The stock attempted a recovery on Friday, gaining approximately 4%, but buyers failed to push it back above the psychological $200 level, leaving shares close to the important $180 support zone. The latest weakness reflects growing concerns about the enormous infrastructure commitments underpinning semiconductor valuations. Investors are increasingly questioning whether major technology companies can maintain their current investment pace as financing costs rise, electricity availability becomes more challenging and political resistance to new data-centre developments gains momentum. The Democratic victories in the US midterm elections have introduced another challenge for Nvidia and the broader semiconductor industry. Gina Hinojosa’s victory in Texas, alongside political changes in Ohio and Georgia involving Amy Acton and Keisha Lance Bottoms, has strengthened opposition to unchecked data-centre expansion. Proposals for restrictions and freezes on new developments highlight growing concerns about electricity consumption, water requirements and rising utility bills. Reports that 40 of 41 direct votes concerning data-centre projects failed further illustrate the changing public sentiment. For Nvidia, the implications could extend beyond political headlines. Delays in construction, additional regulatory requirements and higher infrastructure expenses could affect the spending plans of major cloud providers, which remain among the company’s most important customers. Electricity availability is becoming a significant bottleneck for the infrastructure industry. Technology companies may increasingly need to finance additional power generation and grid improvements rather than relying entirely on existing electricity networks. Financing conditions are also creating pressure. CoreWeave has faced growing scrutiny as yields on some of its debt maturing in 2032 approached 15%, highlighting the risks associated with heavily leveraged infrastructure expansion. Amazon has reportedly experienced delays involving Nvidia-equipped server racks waiting in warehouses because certain data centres lack sufficient electricity to operate them. These developments raise questions about construction schedules, capital efficiency and whether the enormous investments being made will generate sufficient returns. NVIDIA shares lost momentum early in September after failing to break decisively above the $236 resistance zone, with the rejection sending the stock back below $210 but we have seen a decent rebound recently. Shares have climbed above $233 today as investors responded positively to expanding infrastructure partnerships and CEO projections, but buyers are not able to sustain the rally above $243 and we saw dive to $180 today where NVDA is testing the last support at the 100 weekly SMA in green. The trend will depend on whether the 100 SMA holds as support. Despite the share-price weakness, Nvidia continues strengthening its position across the semiconductor supply chain. CEO Jensen Huang reportedly consulted with Marvell Technology and Lumentum executives ahead of Marvell’s approximately $115 billion enterprise-value acquisition of Lumentum. Nvidia previously invested $2 billion in each company, increasing its exposure to optical networking and connectivity technologies required for expanding data-centre infrastructure. However, the transaction also highlights the enormous capital requirements associated with building the next generation of computing infrastructure. Demand for computing capacity remains substantial. Anthropic reportedly plans to increase its computing capacity beyond 3.5 gigawatts by the end of 2026, potentially reaching approximately 7 gigawatts in 2027. Samsung Electronics is also preparing to manufacture base dies for high-bandwidth memory chips intended for Nvidia and AMD, with mass production targeted for 2030. However, Nvidia is facing increasing competition from custom processors. Google and Oracle plan to make Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) available through Oracle Cloud Infrastructure from 2027, providing customers with another alternative to Nvidia-powered systems. Although Nvidia retains considerable advantages through its software ecosystem, performance and established customer relationships, expanding competition could eventually put pressure on pricing and market share. The technical picture has deteriorated significantly following the decline below $200. Friday’s 4% rebound provides some relief, but buyers have yet to reclaim this important psychological level. The immediate focus remains on $180 support. A sustained break below this area could expose further downside towards $150, while a recovery above $200 would be needed to improve the short-term outlook. Nvidia remains a major semiconductor player with substantial exposure to long-term computing demand. Nevertheless, investors are increasingly questioning whether infrastructure spending can continue at its previous pace. For now, sellers retain control of the technical picture, while political opposition, electricity shortages, financing risks and growing competition could keep Nvidia shares under pressure.

Taiwan Semiconductor, the world's largest chip foundry, is considering expanding its business into advanced storage chip manufacturing and has, at the request of its largest customer NVIDIA, begun formulating plans to produce 3D DRAM (three-dimensional dynamic random-access memory). The Zhitong Finance APP has learned that, according to media reports, Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM.US), the world's largest chip foundry, is considering expanding its business into advanced storage chip manufacturing and has, at the request of its largest customer NVIDIA (NVDA.US), begun formulating plans to produce 3D DRAM (three-dimensional dynamic random-access memory). If this plan is ultimately implemented, Taiwan Semiconductor could further expand its influence in the artificial intelligence (AI) hardware supply chain. According to media reports citing two insiders, Taiwan Semiconductor has recently begun studying production plans for 3D DRAM. This move stems from NVIDIA's demand for advanced memory chips and reflects that AI chip designers are actively seeking to diversify their sources of critical components. 3D DRAM is an advanced memory chip technology that employs a three-dimensional architecture, aiming to increase storage density through novel cell layouts and manufacturing processes, while providing more technological options for future high-performance computing systems. For Taiwan Semiconductor, which has long focused on logic chip foundry and advanced packaging, entering advanced DRAM manufacturing would mean further expanding its business portfolio. Currently, Taiwan Semiconductor dominates the global advanced logic chip manufacturing sector and is also a key manufacturing partner for NVIDIA's AI accelerators. If it further enters the advanced memory chip production field in the future, Taiwan Semiconductor will have the opportunity to play a role in more critical segments of AI computing hardware. This potential business expansion comes at a time when the global memory chip market is facing severe supply constraints. As the boom in generative AI and data center construction continues, demand for high-performance computing hardware and associated memory chips is surging, tightening supply and driving prices sharply higher. For AI chip designers such as NVIDIA, memory chips are a critical component that determines the performance and production scale of computing systems. Supply shortages could not only drive up hardware manufacturing costs but also constrain the pace of AI infrastructure deployment. Consequently, major tech companies, including NVIDIA and Apple (AAPL.US), are actively seeking additional sources of memory chip supply to mitigate supply chain risks. The impact of rising storage chip prices has also begun to ripple through the consumer electronics market. Earlier this year, Apple raised the prices of some products, citing higher storage costs, highlighting that the tight supply of storage chips is no longer confined to the AI server sector but is affecting a broader range of electronic product markets. Against this backdrop, NVIDIA is urging Taiwan Semiconductor to research 3D DRAM production, which may help it establish a more diversified advanced storage chip supply system in the future. However, the relevant plans are currently still in the preliminary research and planning stages. The report did not disclose the scale of funding Taiwan Semiconductor plans to invest, its potential production capacity, the mass-production timeline, or whether it will formally launch commercial production in the future. Furthermore, 3D DRAM is not entirely the same technological route as High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), which is widely used in current AI accelerators, and Taiwan Semiconductor's research into 3D DRAM production does not mean it has decided to enter the existing HBM market. Management guided gross margin to a low of 71% to 72% in fiscal Q4 2027, down from 75% in fiscal Q2 2027. For fiscal Q3 2027, it guided gross margin to 74%, plus or minus 50 basis points. The drop matters at NVIDIA’s size. Each point of gross margin on its $303 billion of revenue over the past twelve months is worth about $3 billion a year. title: S&P 500 Or Dividend Stocks: What Mix Fits Your Plan For 2027? - Trefis
content: Part of our series on building a mix that lasts. Start here: is 60/40 dead? S&P 500 or dividend stocks? After a day like Thursday, plenty of people are asking it, and it has a real answer, with numbers on both sides. We’ll give you all of them, stock by stock. But here’s what’s less random than any single day: the mix you pick ahead of time decides how a 4% drop feels, and whether you do something you regret about it. We’ll come back to how to pick yours, and how to know it fits a plan for 2027. “Lose 50% and you need 100% to get back to even. The best way to win is not to lose too much.” – Anonymous The S&P 500 fund (SPY) fell 4.41% to $733.00. The Nasdaq-100 fund (QQQ) fell 6.5%. The dividend funds fell by less: SCHD 2.18% and DGRO 2.77%. The 50 stocks in the Trefis Income Solution, at their October 31 weights, fell 1.5%, about a third of the index’s drop. It was the AI trade unwinding: the chip makers and the companies building the power and data centers behind AI fell hardest. Power is the bottleneck, opposition to new data centers is growing town by town, and the new Congress can lean on both; Meta’s president warned at a Wall Street Journal conference on Wednesday that building new data centers will get harder. We flagged power as the AI trade’s real risk on Nov 2. That’s why the gap was so wide. Seven companies make up about a third of SPY, by State Street’s count as of Nov 4. On Thursday they supplied about a third of its fall, mostly from two chip makers, Nvidia and Broadcom. The Income Solution owns none of them. Neither, on its own, and the data shows why. Start with the record. The Income Solution model holds 50 dividend payers with at least 10 straight years of payments, weighted by size with no stock above 5%. Over the last nine and a half years it behaved like this next to the S&P 500: It gave up 1.7 points a year for a flat 2022, smaller losses in down months and three times the income. Why do the two behave so differently? Look at what’s inside each. Here are four of the biggest stocks in the S&P 500 fund next to four of the biggest in the Income Solution: Trefis data, Nov 5 close; Nvidia’s yield is on its $1.00 annual dividend after May’s raise (0.29% on the past year’s payouts). The index’s leaders sell growth; the dividend names sell steadiness. The prices aren’t the difference. That last line surprises people. Dividend stocks aren’t cheap today: AbbVie trades at about 50 times earnings and Coca-Cola at 28, in the same range as Apple and Microsoft. What you’re choosing between is two kinds of business. Nvidia’s sales are about nine times what they were three years ago. Procter & Gamble’s grew 6% in total. One gives you a shot at the next big leg of the AI build-out, along with days like Thursday. The other gives you a check every quarter and a stock that barely moved on Thursday. Now the case for the index, and it’s just as real. The Income Solution trailed the S&P 500 in 6 of the last 10 calendar years. The big gaps came in strong rallies. In 2023 it rose 1.4% while the index rose 26.2%. Over 2023, 2024 and 2025 together, that’s roughly +23% against +86%. If you’d owned only dividend stocks from 2023 on, you’d have watched the index run away from you for three straight years. That’s hard to sit through too. Here’s the part most comparisons skip, measured on daily closes, dividends included: In the fast 2020 crash, dividend stocks fell nearly as far. In the slow 2022 grind, they fell about half as far and were back 13 months sooner. That’s honest and it matters. When everything is sold at once, as in March 2020, dividend stocks are stocks. The dividend fund SCHD fell 33.4% then, almost exactly as much as SPY. The cushion shows up in the longer, slower declines, which are also the ones that test your patience most. And the quote above is the reason it matters: after a 24.5% fall you need about a 32% gain to get back to even; after a 13.6% fall, about 16%. Here’s the bigger number. Put the two together and the trade-off gets much smaller than either side alone. Over April 2017 to October 2026, rebalanced monthly, on month-end values: The 50/50 mix kept all but about three-quarters of a point a year of the index’s return and cut its 2022 loss by more than half. In dollars: on $1 million, the plain index fund lost about $182,000 in 2022; the 50/50 mix about $81,000. On Thursday the same mix would have lost about $30,000 per million instead of $44,000. Over ten years, giving up three-quarters of a point a year adds up to about 6% less money at the end, if the next ten looked like the last nine and a half, which they may not. That’s the price of the smaller fall. Whether it’s worth paying depends on you, not on the market. Two honest limits. The window starts in 2017, so it holds one 2020 crash and one 2022, but no 2008. And the Income Solution figures are a model, before fees. Not Thursday. What will matter is whether you were still holding your plan when the next good year came. Here’s how to pick a mix you’ll actually keep: 1. Start from what you need the money to do. If you’re spending from the portfolio in 2027, income and a smaller fall carry more weight: on $1 million, a 3.0% yield is about $30,000 a year without selling a share, against about $10,000 from the index. If you won’t touch the money for ten years, the index’s growth matters more. 2. Pick the worst year you can sit through, in dollars. On your real balance, would you hold through a $182,000 loss per million, or an $81,000 one? Be honest. The best mix on paper is the one you won’t sell at the bottom. 3. Also pick the rally you can sit through. This is the part most people skip. If watching the index rise 26% while you rose 1.4% would make you abandon dividends at the top, a 100% dividend portfolio isn’t for you either. 4. Write down a rebalance band. For a 50/50 mix, say 5 points: when one side drifts to 55%, trade back to 50. That takes roughly an 18% gap between the two halves, so most weeks you do nothing. What this replaces: switching from the index to dividend stocks after a bad day, or back again after a strong year. Both chase the last move. The risk: any mix with dividend stocks will trail a plain index fund in a straight-up market, and a crash like 2020 hits dividend stocks nearly as hard as the index. We call it choose the mix before the swing. A mix chosen on a calm day decides how a 4% drop feels before it happens. A mix chosen on a 4% day is usually a reaction to that day. If you want to see how a dividend slice fits next to bonds, gold and cash too, we take that up in our piece on whether 60/40 is dead. Choose the mix, not the winner. Since 2017 the S&P 500 earned 14.6% a year; dividend stocks 12.9% with three times the yield (model, before fees); a 50/50 mix 13.9%, and it lost 8.1% in 2022, not 18.2% (model). The index’s leaders grew sales far faster; the dividend names fell about half as far in 2022 but nearly as far in the 2020 crash. Pick the worst year and the strongest rally you can both sit through, write down a band, and let the plan carry you to 2027. Follow this story with us: we’ll keep tracking how the index and the dividend sleeve do through year end and into 2027. The right split depends on your spending, your taxes and the falls you can live with. title: Will Nvidia Stock Jump 20% In The Next 30 Days? - Trefis
content: Follow the whole story: every piece in this series is on our AI storyline page. Could Nvidia jump 20% in the next 30 days? Yes, it could, and it has done it many times before. We’ll give you the real odds, the numbers behind the business, the dated catalyst and how far it has fallen before. But here’s the number the pros reach for first after a day like Thursday: not where Nvidia trades in December, but how much of it they already own, counting the Nvidia hiding inside their index funds. We’ll come back to it at the end. Nvidia closed Thursday at about $181.60, down about 9.3% from Wednesday’s $200.13. That came on a rough day for everything: the S&P 500 fund SPY fell 4.4% to $733.00 and the Nasdaq-100 fund QQQ 6.5%. The chip makers fell harder still: Broadcom lost about 10% and the chip fund SMH about 11%. It was the AI trade unwinding: the chip makers and the companies building the power and data centers behind AI fell hardest. The worry has been building for weeks. Power is the bottleneck, opposition to new data centers is growing town by town, and the new Congress can lean on both; a Wall Street Journal article argued on Thursday that the backlash could play into the hands of Big Tech. We flagged power as the AI trade’s real risk on Nov 2, in “Nvidia Stock’s Real Risk Isn’t China. It’s Power.” Nvidia had held up earlier in the week while the data-center builders fell hard; whether it is now the dip to buy is the question in should you buy Nvidia stock at $182? Here’s the straight answer from Nvidia’s own history. We looked at every 30-day stretch (21 trading days) in the Trefis price cache and counted how often the stock ended at least 20% higher, or at least 20% lower: A 20% month for Nvidia is uncommon, not rare: roughly 1 in 7 or 8, and about 1 in 6 after a big down day. Those stretches overlap, so treat them as a feel for the odds, not a forecast. The closer match is the last row. Thirty days after Nvidia’s 44 earlier days of 7%+ falls since 2010, it was higher 23 times and lower 21, with a median gain of about 4%. The big rebounds came mostly after the March 2020 crash and the late-2022 bottom; two of the four further 20% falls came in late 2018. So the honest answer: a 20% jump is possible, it has happened after big drops before, and a month after a big down day Nvidia has been close to a coin flip. A 20% jump from about $181.60 gets you to about $218. That’s not a new high. Nvidia closed at $217.94 just seven trading days earlier, on October 27. So the upside case isn’t a moonshot; it’s a return to late October. Whether that’s a fair price depends on the business, and here the numbers are striking: After Thursday, Nvidia trades at about the market’s average multiple, for a company growing sales more than 80% a year. That’s the upside case in one line. The stock went nowhere for a year while the business kept compounding, so the multiple came down; Thursday alone took it from about 25 times earnings at Wednesday’s close to about 23. The other side of the same line: a market that pays an average multiple for 83% growth is telling you it doubts the growth lasts. That doubt is exactly the power and data-center question above. Next to its peers, Nvidia looks neither cheapest nor most expensive, but it has the widest margins of the big designers, Micron’s memory-cycle peak aside: P/E at Thursday’s close; sales growth and margin over the past 12 months. Micron’s low multiple is the warning label on the whole group: memory makers earn their biggest profits at the top of a cycle, and investors price that in. The dated catalyst for Nvidia is its quarterly report: Nvidia’s notice lists Tuesday, Nov 17, after the close. That report, and what the big buyers say about next year’s data-center spending, will move the stock more than anything we can measure now. This belongs right next to the upside case. Here are Nvidia’s biggest falls, measured on dividend-adjusted closes, with how long it took to get back to the old high: Nvidia has lost more than half its value three times since 2007. Once it took more than seven years to get back. The 2018 fall took less than three months to hit bottom and about 14 months more to recover. The 2022 fall went on for almost eleven months, then recovered in about seven. In 2020 and 2022, Nvidia fell harder than SPY and still got back to its old high months before SPY did. The 2008 case is the exception worth remembering: a 2007 buyer waited until 2016. Put those next to today. From the October 6 high of $239.24, a 2020-size fall would mean about $148, a 2018-size fall about $105, and a 2022-size fall about $81. We’re not saying any of those will happen. We’re saying a long-run Nvidia owner has lived through each of them, and your plan should be able to as well. Here’s what’s less random than the next 30 days: how much of your money rides on this one stock. If you own an S&P 500 fund, you own Nvidia whether you bought it or not. Nvidia is 7.30% of SPY, its second-largest holding after Apple. Say you have $1 million, with 70% in an S&P 500 fund and no Nvidia shares at all. You still own about $51,000 of Nvidia, 5.1% of everything. Buy another 5% directly on the dip and you’re at about 10%, and Thursday’s fall alone would have cost you about $9,400 on it. That number is something you can find this weekend and act on. The 30-day move isn’t. And it’s not just Nvidia. Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta, the companies buying Nvidia’s chips, plus Broadcom, add up to about 19% more of SPY. Together with Nvidia that’s roughly 26.5% of the fund riding on one spending boom. Three steps, none of which needs a guess about December. 1. Add up your total Nvidia. Direct shares, plus your S&P 500 fund times 7.30%, plus any Nasdaq-100 or chip fund times its Nvidia weight (about 8% in QQQ and about 20% in SMH in late October). Write down one number, as a share of your portfolio. 2. Set your band before Nov 17. Pick the most you’d want in one stock, say 8% to 10% of your portfolio, and the level that makes you trim, say 12%. If you’re under the band and you believe in the business, add in pieces. If you’re over it, trim back to the band, whatever the price did. 3. Decide what you do after a 2022-size fall. If Nvidia went to about $81, would you buy, hold or sell? Whatever the answer, write it down now, while you’re not looking at a red screen. What this replaces: buying a big chunk on Friday morning because a 20% bounce feels likely, or selling because Thursday hurt. The risk: if Nvidia jumps 20% and you were under your band, you’ll own less of the jump. That’s the price of a plan that also works if it falls another third. A 20% month is a 1-in-7 shot; your exposure is a number. Since 2016, Nvidia rose 20% or more in about 13% of 30-day stretches. After Thursday it trades near the market’s multiple, about 23 times earnings, with sales up 83% and $127 billion of free cash flow, and it has fallen 56% and 66% in the past eight years. Nvidia is 7.30% of SPY, so most investors own more than they think. Add up your total, set a band before the Nov 17 report, and decide now what you’d do after a 2022-size fall. title: The Nasdaq Fell 5% In A Day. What Happened The Last 21 Times? - Trefis
content: Follow the whole story: every piece in this series is on our AI storyline page. The past can’t tell you what Friday does. It can tell you something more useful: whether a plan that holds through days like this has paid off before. We’ll come back to that at the end. Thursday was a rough one. Using the big index funds as stand-ins, the S&P 500 (SPY) fell 4.4% to $733.00 and the Nasdaq-100 (QQQ) 6.5%. The Dow fund and the small-company fund fell less than the Nasdaq, while gold (GLD) and long Treasuries (TLT) edged up. It was the AI trade unwinding: the chip makers and the companies building the power and data centers behind AI fell hardest. The worry has been building for weeks. Power is the bottleneck, opposition to new data centers is growing town by town, and the new Congress can lean on both; on Wednesday, Meta’s president told a Wall Street Journal conference that the midterm results will make building data centers harder. We flagged power as the AI trade’s real risk on Nov 2, in Nvidia Stock’s Real Risk Isn’t China. It’s Power. The damage came from the very top of the market. Ten of the biggest names we track lost roughly $1.5 trillion of market value between them in one session: Nvidia alone lost about as much value as Apple, Alphabet, Meta, Amazon and Microsoft combined. The chip makers lost the most, and the companies that buy their chips lost far less; we take that split apart in Is The AI Trade Officially In Trouble? So here’s the question nearly everyone has after Thursday: is the market overreacting? Nobody can tell you what Friday does. But we can tell you what happened every other time it looked like this. We went through every trading day in the Trefis price cache from December 31, 2002 to November 4, 2026 and kept the days when the S&P 500 fell at least 3.5% and the Nasdaq Composite fell at least 5%. There were 21. Thursday, with the S&P 500 down 4.4% and the Nasdaq Composite down 5.5%, is the 22nd. Days like Thursday travel in packs. Eleven of the 21 came in one stretch, the 2008-09 crisis. A 5% Nasdaq day is rarely alone. In the fall of 2008 there were ten of them in about nine weeks. In March 2020 there were three in eight days. One of the 21 landed on November 5, 2008, the day after a presidential election. Thursday came two days after this year’s midterms. Here’s the S&P 500 after all 21 days, price only, no dividends: The next week and the next three months were close to a coin flip. The next year and the next five were not. A week later the range ran from a further double-digit fall (after March 9, 2020) to a double-digit gain (after November 20, 2008). That’s noise, not a pattern you can trade. Three months later the worst case came after September 29, 2008, with more of that crisis still ahead. Then the picture changes. A year later the index was higher 20 times out of 21, with a median gain of 27%. The one miss was that same September 29, 2008 day, a bit lower a year on. Five years later, for the 18 days old enough to measure, it was higher every time, roughly doubling at the median. Price only: dividends would add to every line. The 2022 and 2025 days aren’t five years old yet, so the five-year row covers 18 days. The days overlap (ten in fall 2008), so this is really five or six episodes, not 21 independent tests. The window starts on December 31, 2002, after the 2000-2002 dot-com fall, so that bear market is not in this data set. Thursday’s figures are the SPY and QQQ funds; the precedents use the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite indexes. A median hides the hard part, so here it is. In each of the last three bear markets, here’s how far the funds and the market’s biggest AI name fell from peak to bottom, and how many months it took to get back to the old high from the bottom, on dividend-adjusted daily prices: Every one of these came all the way back. Some took months, and 2008 took years. Thursday’s drop is small next to any of those rows. Nvidia ended the day about a quarter below its high, against a two-thirds fall in 2022. That doesn’t mean it can’t go lower. It means the history in our first two tables already includes falls far worse than Thursday, and the year-later numbers still came out the way they did. Here’s the honest answer: the data can’t say about this week, and neither can anyone else. What it can say is which question has an answer. “Will it bounce Friday?” had a coin-flip answer 21 times. “Will I be glad I held on a year from now?” had a nearly one-sided answer 21 times. We wrote earlier this week about whether this Nasdaq selloff looks more like 2000 or 2018; that’s the piece to read if your worry is the AI trade itself rather than the market. “We live in decades. Why worry about the next ten minutes like a fruit fly?” – Anonymous Make a plan for the next three months, not a trade for Monday. Three steps: 1. Assume there may be more days like this. In 2008 and 2020 they came in clusters. A week after two of the 21 days the index was already 10% or more lower again. Decide now what you’d do if SPY fell another 10%, to about $660. Write it down. 2. Rebalance by rule, not by mood. If your stocks have drifted well below your target share, a pre-set band tells you when to buy back to it. If they haven’t, you do nothing, and that’s a decision too. 3. Check your chip exposure. Thursday’s biggest falls were in chips. An S&P 500 fund already holds Nvidia, Broadcom, AMD and Micron; Nvidia and Broadcom alone are about a tenth of SPY. Count them before adding more. The risk: the worst three-month case in the data was another 21% fall. A plan doesn’t prevent that; it means you’ve already decided what you do inside it. What it replaces: selling after a 5% day, or buying everything at once because “it always bounces.” It didn’t always bounce within a week. What to watch: whether more 5% days follow in a cluster, and Nvidia’s quarterly report later this month. Both are reasons to check your plan, not to trade. We call it Plan, don’t react. The scariest day in a year is rarely the one that decides the year. Of the 21 days like Thursday since 2002, the one that hurt most a year later came in the thick of the 2008 crisis, and even it was 53% higher five years on. The short run is loud. The long run, in this data, was kinder. History says Thursday’s drop told you little about next week and a lot about how to plan. After the 21 earlier days like it, the S&P 500 was higher a week later only 10 times and three months later 12 times, but a year later 20 times, median +27% (price only). The bear markets around them took SPY 5 to 41 months to recover. Plan for more rough days, rebalance by rule, and judge this by where you’ll be in a year, not on Friday. Follow this story with us: if more days like Thursday come, we’ll add them to the table and show what changed. The next three months may be rough; your plan doesn’t have to be. title: Is The AI Trade Officially In Trouble? - Trefis
content: Follow the whole story: every piece in this series is on our AI storyline page. Short answer: a day like Thursday isn’t trouble. Trouble has a definition, and it’s simple: the four big buyers of AI chips cutting what they plan to spend in 2027. Until that happens, a 9% day is a price story, not a business story. The question that will still matter next year is a quieter one: how much of your money rides on AI, counting your index fund too? We’ll come back to it. That it was an ugly day. SPY fell 4.4% and QQQ 6.5%. It was the AI trade unwinding: the chip makers and the companies building the power and data centers behind AI fell hardest. Power is the bottleneck, opposition to new data centers is growing town by town, and the new Congress can lean on both; a Wall Street Journal article argued on Thursday that the backlash could play into the hands of Big Tech. We flagged it on Nov 2, in “Nvidia Stock’s Real Risk Isn’t China. It’s Power.” The AI trade has two sides: the companies that sell the build-out (chips, power gear, cooling) and the four that pay for it. Thursday split them cleanly: The sellers fell about 12% on average; the buyers about 3%. In dollars, the sellers lost roughly $940 billion of market value and the buyers about $350 billion. Look at the last column. The hardest falls came where the biggest gains had been: Micron had more than tripled in a year and AMD had nearly doubled. Nvidia, the face of the trade, was flat over the 12 months even before Thursday. And Vertiv now sits about half below its high. On Wednesday the market paid the buyers for spending less: they rose while Nvidia fell 3.2%. We wrote up that trade in why Amazon and Google stock rose. On Thursday nobody got paid; the buyers just fell far less. Put the two days together and Nvidia is down about 12% from Tuesday’s close, while the four buyers, on average, are up about 1%. That’s investors betting that if spending slows, the suppliers get hurt and the buyers keep the cash. It’s a guess about the future, priced in two days. It isn’t news about the businesses: the latest spending plans are still the ones the four gave with their results in late October. So let’s look at the businesses. Here’s the classic Trefis check on all eleven: what you pay, how fast sales are growing, and whether profit margins are holding. P/E is at Thursday’s close; growth and margins are over the last 12 reported months. All eleven are growing. Of the ten with five years of history, nine earn margins at or above their five-year average; Meta is the exception, and only by two points. That isn’t what a business in trouble looks like. A few things stand out. Nvidia traded at about 25 times earnings before Thursday and about 23 after, less than Microsoft, while growing sales several times faster. Micron, at about 9 times, is priced as if its margins won’t last: they’re running at more than three times its five-year average. AMD, at nearly 90 times, is the one priced for a lot to go right. The risk in these stocks is the price you pay for growth that has to keep coming, not growth that has stopped. This is the real question under the AI trade, because the buyers’ spending is the sellers’ revenue. Here’s their capital spending story in one table: The four plan to spend more this year than their businesses brought in over the past year. In that year they kept about $61 billion of free cash between them. Nvidia alone kept $127 billion. That last line is the whole story. The money hasn’t vanished; it has moved down the chain, from the buyers’ cash flow to the sellers’ profits. For scale, the seven sellers in our table took in about $660 billion of revenue over the past year, less than the four buyers plan to spend in 2026. Not every capex dollar lands with these seven, but it shows who depends on whom. And the buyers say they aren’t done. Alphabet has said its spending will rise “significantly” in 2027 and Amazon “meaningfully”; Microsoft says it expects to stay free-cash-flow positive while it builds. Amazon is the one already spending more cash than it makes. There’s a twist, too. If towns and states slow new data centers, the capacity that’s already built gets scarcer, and the four buyers own a great deal of it. A pause can hurt the builders and help the incumbents at the same time. One thing: the buyers spending less on AI next year than they said. If two or more of the four hold 2027 spending flat or cut it, the build-out is slowing, and that’s the moment to revisit your plan. Two dates bring real data: Nvidia reports its quarter on Nov 17, and the four buyers report in late January and early February, with their 2027 plans. A second, earlier tell sits in the tables above: if the buyers’ revenue growth slows while their spending keeps climbing, their free cash flow shrinks further, and pressure to cut rises. A red Thursday isn’t either of those. Lower than this, even with the business fine. Here’s how far each fell in the 2022 bear market, how many months it took to get back to its old high from the bottom, and the 2008 fall for those old enough: In 2022 the buyers kept spending, and Nvidia still lost two-thirds of its value. Thursday left it about a quarter below its high. That’s the honest frame for a day like Thursday. A price can fall much further than this without anything breaking in the business, and it can take a year or more to come back. Which is why the plan below is about size, not prediction. “A falling price tells you how other people feel. The business tells you what it is worth.” – Anonymous 1. Count your AI, all of it. Your direct shares, plus what’s inside your index funds, plus the builders and power names that ride the same spending. Nvidia, Broadcom and the four buyers alone are about a quarter of an S&P 500 fund. Most people who count this way find more than they thought; we show how in how much AI you really own. 2. Set a band, not a target. Pick the share you want in AI, then a range around it. For example, a 25% target with a band of 20% to 30%. Above 30%, trim. Below 20%, add. Inside the band, do nothing. 3. Let the band decide, not the day. The move this replaces is selling after a 9% chip day, or buying everything on the dip. If Thursday pushed your count below the band, the rule says add, at prices you already decided were fair. If you’re still above it after Thursday, you were too heavy before Thursday. The risk: if this turns into a 2022-style fall, a band still loses money. You’ll buy on the way down and the price can keep falling, as the table above shows. What the band does is cap how much of your money is exposed, so the loss is one you planned for. Two ideas, really. Exposure hides in plain sight: your index fund owned every side of Thursday’s trade, the sellers and the buyers. And price isn’t the business: a day like Thursday for AMD tells you how other investors felt that day; the buyers’ 2027 plans and their cash flow will tell you what the business is worth. Watch the plans, size by the band, and let the price do what prices do. The AI trade isn’t officially in trouble; it’s officially volatile. The sellers fell about four times as much as the buyers on Thursday, yet all eleven are growing revenue and nine of ten are running at or above their five-year margins. The buyers plan about $730 billion of 2026 capex, and Alphabet and Amazon have said 2027 goes higher. Trouble is two or more of the four holding 2027 spending flat or lower, which you’ll see in late January. Until then, count your total AI exposure, set a band, and rebalance only when the count crosses it. Follow this story with us: we’ll be back after Nvidia’s report and again when the buyers set their 2027 plans, with what changed and what didn’t. Thursday tests the plan, not the trade. title: Should You Buy Nvidia Stock At $182? - Trefis
content: Follow the whole story: every piece in this series is on our AI storyline page. Democrats won both chambers on Tuesday, and Texas elected a governor who has called for a pause on new data centers. On Wednesday the market treated that as a brake on AI building. The stocks that power and cool data centers fell hardest: Vertiv −12.9%, Vistra −13.8%, Eaton −9.9%, GE Vernova −9.3%. The companies that pay for the buildings rose: Microsoft +6.7%, Amazon +6.1%, Alphabet +3.2%, Meta +1.4%. Nvidia, which sells them the chips, closed at $200.13, down 3.2%. On Thursday Nvidia fell another 9.3%, to $181.60. On Wednesday alone the gap between the buyers and their supplier was about 7.5 points. The four buyers rose 4.4% on average, equal-weighted, while Nvidia fell 3.2%. That’s the trade in one line: less building means more cash for the buyers and less revenue for the seller. It only works if the building actually slows. Broadcom −2.0%, CoreWeave −9.9%, Constellation Energy −6.7%; AMD rose 1.0% after its record-quarter report on Tuesday. Nvidia had already fallen 7.1% over five days and 16% over a month by Wednesday’s close, on doubts about whether AI spending pays off, doubts that are older than the vote. That it is cheaper than the companies that buy from it, on the cash it actually makes: The four biggest buyers made about $61 billion of free cash together. Nvidia made about $127 billion by itself. That isn’t a coincidence. The buyers’ capital spending is a large part of Nvidia’s revenue, which grew 83% over the last year to about $303 billion, with an operating margin of 65%. So when investors cheer “less capex” at Amazon or Alphabet, they’re also cheering less revenue at Nvidia. Nvidia trades at about 23 times its last year’s earnings, below Microsoft and well below Broadcom and AMD. Free cash flow is each company’s free-cash-flow margin times its revenue over the last twelve reported months, from Trefis market data: Nvidia 41.9% of $303.0B; Microsoft 17.3% of $346.4B; Meta 11.9% of $241.6B; Alphabet 4.2% of $471.1B; Amazon −5.9% of $797.5B; Broadcom 44.2% of $89.1B; AMD 15.5% of $45.4B. The four buyers total about $61B. At Thursday’s close, Nvidia’s free cash flow trades at about 35 times, a 2.9% yield. Not easily, and not first. Each of the four is spending because it fears falling behind the other three; whoever cuts first hands the others its customers. We laid out that trap in why Big Tech can’t stop spending on AI. Their own words point the same way: Alphabet says its spending will rise “significantly” in 2027 and Amazon “meaningfully”. A state pause in Texas moves a data center to another state; it doesn’t cancel the chips inside it. So the question isn’t whether Nvidia beats its buyers by February. Nobody knows that, and a long-run investor doesn’t need to. The question is what price you’d be glad to own it at if the spending keeps rising, and how much of your money should ride on it if it doesn’t. Two dates bring new data: Nvidia’s report on Nov 17, and the four buyers’ 2027 spending plans in late January and early February. Neither is a reason to trade. Both are reasons to check your plan. For reference, Thursday’s close: Nvidia $181.60, Amazon $260.21, Microsoft $535.93, Alphabet $282.57, Meta $605.08. Further than you’d like. In our look at how low AI chip stocks could go, a drop the size of chip stocks’ 2022 fall would put Nvidia near $129, about 29% below Thursday’s close. Three things could get it there: The next test comes sooner: Nvidia reports its quarter on Nov 17. 1. Decide your price before you decide yes or no. If you’d only want Nvidia meaningfully cheaper than $182, say how much cheaper and write it down now, not after the next 10% move. 2. Get paid to wait for it. One example, for education only: a cash-secured put at a $170 strike expiring May 21, 2027, about six months out, paid about $16.90 a share at Thursday’s close (midpoint of the bid and ask), an effective entry near $153, about 16% below Thursday’s close. Per contract you set aside $17,000 and collect about $1,690. The risk: if Nvidia falls to our $129 worst case, you still buy at $170, about $2,400 per contract worse than buying at that low, after the premium. 3. Count what you already own. An S&P 500 fund already holds Nvidia and all four of its buyers, worth about $16 trillion together. If adding Nvidia takes your AI share past your target, skip step 2. This is education, not personal advice; options aren’t right for every account. We call it Exposure hides in plain sight. A buyer’s spending is its supplier’s revenue. On Wednesday the market bought Amazon and Alphabet for spending less and sold Nvidia for the same reason, and an index fund owned both sides of that bet. Before you buy a dip, ask what has to be true for it to be a dip and not a new, lower price. Here it’s one thing: the four keep spending. You’ll know in February. Nvidia at $182 is a reasonable price, not an obvious bargain. It trades at about 23 times earnings, below Microsoft, and makes twice the free cash flow of its four biggest buyers combined. Wednesday priced in spending cuts that Alphabet and Amazon say aren’t coming. Don’t chase it and don’t dump it: decide your price below $182, keep your AI share inside your band, and let Nvidia’s report and the February spending plans tell you whether to revisit the plan. Follow this story with us: after Nvidia’s report and the February spending plans, we’ll come back with what changed for a long-run holder, and what didn’t. Elections change the odds, not your plan. content: U.S. stock indices ended lower on Thursday, with futures extending declines after hours as investors heavily sold off tech and chipmaker stocks amid concerns a Democratic win could derail the pace of data center and AI buildout, delaying capex recovery. The S&P 500 ended Thursday 4.4% lower, the Nasdaq 100 fell 6.4%, well in correction territory, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 3.4%. The Russell 2000, which tracks small-cap stocks, lost 4.5%. S&P 500 futures lost 0.8%, while Nasdaq-100 futures slid 1.3%. Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 264 points, or 0.5%. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) fell 4.5%, and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (DIA) dropped 3.5%. Meanwhile, the Nasdaq-100 tracking Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) ended 6.5% lower on Thursday. Meanwhile, the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) and the iShares Semiconductor ETF dropped between 11% and 12% each on Thursday amid weakness in Nvidia (NVDA), Micron Tech (MU),Broadcom (AVGO) and memory chip maker SanDisk (SNDK). The broader Vanguard Information Technology ETF (VGT) dropped 5.8%. Retail sentiment on Stocktwits for SPY, QQQ, and DIA was ‘bearish.’ The sudden acceleration in the tech selloff was heavily catalyzed by the outcome of Tuesday's midterm elections, which saw Democrats capture majorities in both the Senate and the House of Representatives. Electoral campaigns increasingly centered around public pushback against massive data center developments, driven by community anxieties over escalating electricity costs, environmental strains, and grid reliability. In Texas, newly elected Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa amplified these regional concerns by advocating for an immediate moratorium on new data center construction. Because data centers serve as the physical backbone for AI infrastructure—packed densely with rows of advanced semiconductors—any regulatory roadblock or deceleration in data center spending threatens to translate into severe long-term headwinds for chipmakers. Investors are “stepping away until they get a better sense of the implications of the midterms around the AI capex cycle in particular, which is the biggest economic tailwind we’ve had going for us for the last, call it, three years,” Tim Holland, chief investment officer at Orion, told CNBC. “It’s about tone and tenor from the party that did really well, incredibly well, at the federal level and at the state level.” Moreover, Big Short fame Michael Burry sold 25% of his put positions in the $58 billion VanEck Semiconductor ETF amid the deep sellout seen in tech shares. “The SMH put positions even after the sale, however, have become very large positions,” he wrote. Nvidia is pursuing a plan to turn existing telecom facilities into small AI data centers as a way to deploy its chips more quickly and sidestep growing local resistance to new construction, The Information reported on Thursday. Apple Inc. (AAPL) is set to raise about $7.5 billion from a high-grade bond offering, Bloomberg reported. Shares of DoorDash (DASH) slumped 10% on Thursday after rivals Amazon (AMZN) and Uber Technologies (UBER) struck a partnership giving Amazon Prime members free delivery on Uber Eats restaurant orders of $25 or more when placed directly through Amazon’s website or app. Yucca Growth Infrastructure LLC, the firm building power infrastructure for Oracle Corp.’s (ORCL) New Mexico data center, has reportedly agreed to waive a looming regulatory deadline, instead of risking an application denial. Apple Inc. (AAPL) is set to raise about $7.5 billion from a high-grade bond offering, Bloomberg reported on Thursday. The transaction drew substantial interest from investors, pulling in roughly $31 billion in total orders—more than four times the ultimate size of the deal, as per Bloomberg. The corporate debt issuance comes during a turbulent period for global financial markets. Institutional investors are pricing in heightened regulatory scrutiny and potential zoning, environmental, or power supply delays regarding massive AI data center construction projects in the wake of the U.S. midterm election outcomes, Concerns are mounting over the pace of AI monetization. Global capital expenditures on AI hardware are projected to approach $900 billion, and Wall Street is increasingly demanding proof that enterprise revenues will justify these massive infrastructure outlays before committing more capital. title: NVDA Stock Faces the Last Support as Midterm Elections Put Data-Centre Spending and Nvidia Under Pressure - FXLeaders
content: Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) stock has fallen below $200 to around $181, extending their retreat from record highs above $243 as Democratic victories in the US midterm elections intensify concerns about data-centre expansion, electricity shortages, financing costs and growing political opposition to the technology infrastructure boom. Nvidia shares have suffered another sharp reversal after failing to sustain their recover. The stock initially rebounded towards $210 last week, supported by improving geopolitical sentiment, but renewed selling pressure has pushed shares down to approximately $181. The latest decline reflects growing concerns about the enormous infrastructure commitments underpinning semiconductor valuations. Investors are increasingly questioning whether technology companies can maintain their current investment pace as financing costs rise, electricity availability becomes more challenging and political resistance to new data centers gains momentum. Nvidia has now retreated significantly from its record above $243, with the immediate technical picture deteriorating. The $180 area is the next important support zone, while a decisive break lower could expose further downside towards $150. Buyers would need to reclaim $200 to improve the immediate outlook and restore confidence in a recovery. The Democratic victories in the US midterm elections have introduced a new political risk for Nvidia and the wider semiconductor industry. Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Greg Abbott in Texas, becoming the state’s first Democratic governor in more than three decades. Her campaign included a proposal for an immediate freeze on new data-centre developments. Similar opposition has emerged in Ohio and Georgia, where Governor-elect Amy Acton and Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms have also called for greater restrictions on unchecked infrastructure expansion. The election results highlight a broader shift in public sentiment. Reports indicate that 40 of 41 direct votes concerning data-centre projects failed, while several candidates supporting rapid expansion also lost their races. This creates a difficult environment for technology companies that have committed enormous amounts of capital to infrastructure construction. There are several reasons why investors are reassessing the sector: Political opposition: Local communities are increasingly resisting new data centres because of concerns about electricity consumption, water requirements and the impact on household utility bills. Electricity shortages: Power infrastructure may struggle to accommodate the pace of planned construction, potentially delaying projects and reducing the returns on invested capital. Higher construction costs: Companies could be forced to finance additional electricity generation and supporting infrastructure rather than relying entirely on existing power grids. Spending discipline: Investors are beginning to reward technology companies that demonstrate greater capital discipline rather than simply increasing infrastructure budgets. For Nvidia, this is particularly important because its future revenue expectations remain heavily dependent on continued spending by major cloud providers. NVIDIA shares lost momentum early in September after failing to break decisively above the $236 resistance zone, with the rejection sending the stock back below $210 but we have seen a decent rebound recently. Shares have climbed above $233 today as investors responded positively to expanding infrastructure partnerships and CEO projections, but buyers are not able to sustain the rally above $243 and we saw dive to $180 today where NVDA is testing the last support at the 100 weekly SMA in yellow. Despite the deteriorating share price, Nvidia continues to expand its influence across the semiconductor supply chain. CEO Jensen Huang’s reported involvement in Marvell Technology’s acquisition of Lumentum Holdings highlights the company’s strategic relationships with infrastructure suppliers. According to Bloomberg, Marvell CEO Matthew Murphy and Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston consulted Huang before announcing the transaction, which values Lumentum at approximately $115 billion in enterprise value. Nvidia previously invested $2 billion in each company, strengthening its exposure to optical networking and data-centre connectivity. However, the enormous transaction also highlights the capital requirements associated with expanding the infrastructure supporting advanced computing. Not all developments point towards a slowdown. Reports indicate that Anthropic plans to increase its computing capacity beyond 3.5 gigawatts by the end of 2026, potentially reaching approximately 7 gigawatts in 2027. This demonstrates that demand for computing infrastructure remains substantial, providing support for Nvidia’s longer-term growth prospects. Samsung Electronics is also reportedly preparing to manufacture base dies for high-bandwidth memory chips intended for Nvidia and AMD at its second foundry facility in Taylor, Texas. Construction is expected to begin this month, with mass production targeted for 2030. Nevertheless, strong demand projections do not necessarily guarantee that infrastructure projects will be completed on schedule or generate sufficient returns. Competition is another challenge for Nvidia. Google and Oracle have announced plans to make Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) available through Oracle Cloud Infrastructure from 2027. This provides customers with another alternative to Nvidia-powered systems as major technology companies attempt to reduce computing costs and dependence on external suppliers. Nvidia maintains considerable advantages through its established software ecosystem, performance and customer relationships. However, the expansion of custom processors could eventually pressure pricing and market share, even if overall computing demand continues growing. Financing conditions are becoming increasingly important for the semiconductor industry. CoreWeave has experienced significant pressure as yields on its debt maturing in 2032 climbed towards 15%, highlighting the risks associated with heavily leveraged infrastructure expansion. Electricity shortages are also creating deployment problems. Amazon reportedly has Nvidia-equipped server racks waiting in warehouses because some data centres lack sufficient electricity to operate them. Such delays could increase storage costs and postpone revenue generation from infrastructure investments, raising further questions about the returns expected from the current spending cycle. Nvidia remains one of the strongest companies in the semiconductor industry, with substantial customer relationships and exposure to long-term computing demand. However, the market is increasingly questioning whether infrastructure spending can continue expanding at the pace previously anticipated. The Democratic election victories have brought political opposition to data-centre construction into the mainstream, adding to concerns about electricity availability, financing costs and competition. Technically, the decline below $200 represents a significant setback. The $180 level is now critical, with a sustained break potentially opening the door towards $150. A recovery above $200 would be needed to improve the immediate technical picture. For now, sellers remain in control. Despite continued demand for advanced processors, Nvidia shares could remain under pressure as investors demand stronger evidence that the enormous infrastructure investments supporting current valuations will generate sustainable returns.

title: US Futures Mixed After Rally On Wednesday — MU, TSLA, AAPL, MSFT, APP, NVDA, IREN In Focus - Stocktwits
content: U.S. equity futures were mixed early on Thursday after the previous session's rally, helped by a sharp drop in oil prices and greater clarity following Democrats’ midterm victories. As of 3.45 a.m. ET, S&P 500 futures fell 0.11%, while Nasdaq-100 futures declined around 1%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures moved in the opposite direction, gaining 0.5%. The cautious start followed a strong session on Wednesday, when major U.S. indexes closed higher as technology and semiconductor stocks rebounded. The S&P 500 ended 2% higher on Wednesday, while the Nasdaq-100 advanced 1%. The Dow climbed 3% to its highest level in a year. The small-cap Russell 2000 also added 1.6%. Oil prices rebounded in early Thursday trading after initially extending their losses, as investors weighed whether Republicans’ setbacks in this week's congressional elections could lower the risk of further escalation in the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. Brent crude futures rose around 1.05% to $95.61 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude gained 0.3% to $88.38 as of 3:45 a.m. ET. The recovery followed a sharp sell-off on Wednesday, when both benchmarks plunged more than 8% to settle at their lowest levels since August 31. Micron Technology (MU): Micron came under pressure in early premarket trading on Thursday, with shares down over 3% as concerns about tighter AI regulation compounded weakness across technology stocks. Democratic Rep. Yassamin Ansari of Arizona called on Wednesday for a pause in advanced AI development until adequate regulations are in place. The prospect of stricter rules has raised concerns that congressional action could slow data center expansion and limit demand for AI computing capacity. Tesla (TSLA): A potential Tesla-SpaceX merger is facing fresh questions as political pressure on Elon Musk adds to concerns about regulatory hurdles and the value of any takeover premium. Mark Tepper, CEO of Strategic Wealth Partners, raised doubts about the prospects of such a deal, stating that greater scrutiny of Musk could create challenges for both companies. His comments followed Democrats' victories in both chambers of Congress and the Texas governor's race. Texas is home to major Tesla and SpaceX operations, as well as their planned Terafab chipmaking project. Tesla shares had dropped 3% on Wednesday, taking their weekly losses to nearly 4%, and were down 2.2% in early premarket trading on Thursday. Apple (AAPL): Apple crossed the $5-trillion valuation mark on Wednesday as its shares climbed to a 52-week high, supported by optimism around its earnings outlook and stronger device demand. Investors have also responded positively to expectations of improving cost conditions and the company's upbeat revenue forecast. The stock gave up some ground in early premarket trading on Thursday, slipping 0.15% at the time of writing. Microsoft (MSFT): Microsoft's latest earnings and continued growth in its Azure cloud business helped drive the stock to a 52-week high on Wednesday. Adding to the optimism, Bill Ackman's Pershing Square said in its third-quarter investor letter that Microsoft is well-positioned to benefit from growing AI adoption through Azure, Copilot, and GitHub. The stock was up 0.08% in early premarket trading on Thursday. AppLovin (APP): The stock was among the biggest premarket gainers on Thursday after the advertising technology company reported record third-quarter results on Wednesday. Revenue jumped 55% year over year, while net income rose 72%. The stock had already gained 10% during Wednesday's regular session and climbed around 18% in Thursday’s premarket trading. Nvidia (NVDA): Nvidia faced renewed pressure as concerns over tighter AI regulations and possible delays in data center projects weighed on semiconductor stocks. The prospect of stricter rules under the incoming political landscape has raised questions about the pace of AI infrastructure spending. Investors are also debating the sustainability of the sector's rapid expansion, including concerns over circular financing and off-balance-sheet debt used to fund large AI hardware purchases. Nvidia shares were down around 1% in early premarket trading on Thursday. IREN (IREN): The stock remained on traders' radar after coming under heavy selling pressure on Wednesday, with shares plunging 11.4% during the regular session. The decline came as cloud and AI stocks faced pressure following Democrats' midterm victory. The company also faced scrutiny after a report linked its business to Microsoft's lower AI capital spending in the previous quarter. IREN shares fell around 1.3% in early premarket trading on Thursday. Fastly (FSLY), Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), and Credo Technology (CRDO) were among the other trending tickers on Stocktwits at the time of writing on Thursday. Investors will be tracking a fresh batch of corporate earnings, with DraftKings (DKNG), Novavax (NVAX), GoPro (GPRO), Tapestry (TPR), Airbnb (ABNB) and Akamai (AKAM) among the companies scheduled to report on Thursday. Meanwhile, weekly jobless claims will be in focus on Thursday, ahead of the October nonfarm payrolls report due on Friday. Retail sentiment showed mixed trends across major index ETFs over the past 24 hours. Sentiment toward SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), which tracks the S&P 500, improved to ‘bearish’ from ‘extremely bearish,’ while for Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ), which tracks the Nasdaq 100, it remained ‘bearish’. Meanwhile, sentiment toward the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) turned ‘bullish’ from ‘neutral’. Arthur Hayes expects "insiders unlock and dump" to flood SpaceX (SPCX) stock, then follow suit with Anthropic (ANT) and OpenAI (OPEAZZX), triggering a credit squeeze that ends in a central bank bailout that lifts crypto and makes Bitcoin (BTC) ‘glorious’ in the long run. Hayes made the case Thursday in a Substack essay called "D For Dilution." In his essay, he said the three companies' stocks would struggle as locked-up shares held by insiders become free to trade. Then falling share prices will make it harder for the companies to borrow, tightening the dollar liquidity crypto depends on, Hayes wrote. "This presents an issue for the general market environment because the entire AI trade rests on vibes. The vibes surrounding whether you believe the lofty future profitability and ubiquity of AI determine whether you lend money to the industry," Hayes added. Hayes compared the setup to Zcash (ZEC) back in 2016. Early adopters bought at high prices with a small amount of the token available, and most are still underwater even as Zcash's market value has grown since. You don't trade the market cap; you trade the price per token," he wrote. ZEC’s price was up over 2%, trading around $1,318. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around ZEC remained in the ‘bearish’ zone, accompanied by ‘normal’ chatter levels over the past day. SpaceX's stock price has been relatively stable since its initial public offering, but the number of publicly traded shares has increased by about 50%, Hayes said. He projected that some 8.6 billion additional shares will be available by the end of June 2027. That would increase the float by roughly another 50%, mostly because of the vesting of the shares held by Elon Musk. The rumored combination of SpaceX and Tesla (TSLA) could mean about a 50% dilution for Class A shareholders, Hayes said. The stock can only be supported with an increase in free cash flow, Hayes said. He also said Musk would have to return that cash through dividends or buybacks. Anthropic filed its S-1, the registration statement a company submits to U.S. regulators before an IPO, in late October and intends to go public on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. An AI agent looked at the filing on his behalf, Hayes said. There's no near-term dividend expectation, he said, and the company will plow its money into about $900 billion of compute commitments. Based on that schedule, Hayes wrote, "it is almost impossible mathematically for the stock price to go up between listing and June 2027." He figured that the selloff would take about $1.245 trillion in new money to absorb the price if Anthropic is valued at $1.5 trillion at market. Hayes also said investors should think of Anthropic as an oil and gas company rather than a software company, given customers pay for usage and past spending doesn't guarantee future demand. This comes as investors were already pushing ANT's IPO valuation from $ 1.6 trillion to $2 trillion. Hayes said OpenAI "will be the worst of the bunch." Hayes said that OpenAI has a more concentrated customer base and a higher burn rate than Anthropic. He noted reports that the company had cut its fundraising target from $30 billion to $20 billion and its valuation from $1.5 trillion to $1.25 trillion. Hayes believes a future OpenAI IPO would be structured similarly to SpaceX and Anthropic, with a small float and heavy insider sales in the months ahead. Companies can't borrow money in the debt markets on their own. They have to be publicly traded, Hayes said. If their shares fall, lenders will demand higher yields. That would eat into those loans, Hayes said, who said bank loans powered the crypto rally that began in August. Last week, the U.S. bank balance sheets contracted, we observed. "This is the transmission channel from AI to crypto." His family office, Maelstrom, will stay clear, said Hayes. He believes the central banks will print money once the AI slump turns into a crisis threat. That, he said, "will be glorious for Bitcoin and crypto holders. But be patient." AMC Entertainment Holdings (AMC) stock is heading for its best weekly gain since July, after the theater chain posted record third-quarter (Q3) revenue and Adjusted EBITDA, and CEO Adam Aron declared on X that AMC “has recovered”—a stock attempting to claw back four years of losses. AMC Entertainment stock traded over 2% lower overnight, ahead of Thursday. The stock has gained 15% so far this week and is on track to reverse four years of losses. The rally tests whether a record quarter can change how Wall Street prices a company that spent years as a survival story. AMC still reported a nine-month GAAP net loss, and its stock trades at a valuation unlike its peers’. Aron is betting that a $10 billion-plus box office makes the old debt and dilution worries obsolete. For the better part of four years, AMC Entertainment’s story was about staying alive. This week, its CEO argued that story is over. “Today, we can finally say that AMC has recovered,” Aron posted on X after the company reported Q3 results on Wednesday. He called the quarter “a triumph” and said AMC’s biggest and best in its 106-year history. The numbers back him on growth. Q3 revenue rose 31.6% year-on-year to $1.711 billion, up from $1.300 billion last year. Adjusted EBITDA jumped 183.7% to $347.5 million, nearly triple last year’s figure. Adjusted EBITDA margin hit a record 20.3%, more than double the 9.4% from a year ago. It was the second straight quarter in which AMC set all-time company records for both revenue and Adjusted EBITDA. Analysts had expected about $1.62 billion in revenue and earnings of $0.10 a share, according to Fiscal.ai estimates cited by Stocktwits. AMC reported adjusted earnings of $0.13, against a loss of 58 cents a year ago. Operating cash flow was $176.6 million, versus a $14.9 million outflow a year ago. Free cash flow was $109.3 million, which brings the year-to-date total to $124.7 million. That is why Aron sees AMC posting positive free cash flow for all of 2026. Cash and equivalents more than doubled to $751.9 million, excluding $39.6 million in restricted cash. Attendance did the heavy lifting. Q3 attendance rose 28.3% to 74.9 million moviegoers, with international markets up 41.5% and U.S. markets up 23.3%. AMC did this with slightly fewer screens, averaging 9,177 versus 9,354 a year ago. The company also reported record revenue per patron, which Aron credited to its loyalty programs and its growing roster of premium large-format auditoriums. Aron also leaned on the balance sheet. On Oct. 5, AMC completed a $3.97 billion refinancing covering about 97% of its debt, pushing maturities out to late 2031 and 2033. During the Q3 earnings call, Aron addressed critics directly. He called any future article describing AMC as overly debt-laden “mindlessly in error.” He said “groundless fears of endless share dilution will come only from those looking in the rearview mirror.” He did not rule out new stock sales, saying AMC will “wisely utilize equity financings when it makes sense.” His argument rests on the macro backdrop. AMC now operates in a box office above $10 billion, he said, “a very different animal” from the $7 billion to $9 billion range of the past four years. Q4 looks strong so far. Aron said October’s domestic box office ran about 35% above the same month last year. The remaining slate includes The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, Dune: Part Three, Avengers: Doomsday and Jumanji: Open World. He expects the domestic and global box office to reach their highest full-year levels in seven years. AMC has gained about 125% in 2026 as of late October, ahead of IMAX (IMAX), Cinemark (CNK) and streaming giant Netflix (NFLX). Even with record quarters, its first nine months produced a net loss of $19.2 million, or $0.03 share. Nine-month adjusted net earnings were a modest $26.9 million. Until GAAP profits become consistent, valuation arguments for AMC will rest on EBITDA and cash flow rather than earnings. The next few months will decide whether this week’s 15% gain is the start of a re-rating. The stock has registered a 192% increase in message volume over the past week. Another user said, “$109.3 million in quarterly free cash flow with expectation for positive free cash flow for all of 2026! Stay Zen AMC family. Our time will come.” AMC stock has gained 40% in the past twelve months. Read Next: Why Did AAPL, MSFT, AMC Stocks Surge To 52-Week Highs? SpaceX’s (SPCX) wireless expansion and AI financing, Rocket Lab’s (RKLB) 99th Electron launch and AST SpaceMobile’s (ASTS) Chilean approval have driven space-sector news so far this week, alongside mixed earnings from Redwire (RDW) and Voyager Technologies (VOYG). SpaceX’s mobile ambitions moved forward with Qualcomm’s selection to power Starlink Mobile’s nationwide terrestrial 5G network. Deployment begins in 2027, with tens of thousands of sites planned. “This is a significant win for our infrastructure business and the beginning of a strategic relationship with tremendous potential,” Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon said. The chipmaker expects revenue to begin near the end of fiscal 2027 and develop more fully in fiscal 2028. SpaceX also reportedly explored buying EchoStar’s Boost Mobile or accessing its network, though transferring leased network access could require carrier consent. Alongside its wireless expansion, SpaceX is financing a larger AI buildout. Goldman Sachs and Apollo are seeking buyers for portions of its $40 billion chip financing, covering leased Nvidia Vera Rubin equipment expected in the first half of 2027. SemiAnalysis said SpaceX’s 13GW computing-capacity target for 2027 looked achievable, identifying more than 9GW across sites and 3.6GW under construction, while flagging power constraints. Sequoia partner Shaun Maguire, whose firm backs SpaceX, projected $731.1 billion in 2028 revenue in his investor model. “I think we can do better,” CEO Elon Musk replied. Morgan Stanley separately brought forward its projected free-cash-flow breakeven to 2031 from 2035. However, Musk’s growth ambitions face political and deal risks. Sen.Ted Cruz warned of subpoenas targeting Musk, while Gary Black cautioned that falling shares in an all-stock acquirer could erode the target shareholders’ takeover premium. Retail sentiment for SPCX improved to ‘neutral’ from ‘bearish’ last week, amid ‘high’ message volume. Shares are down 16% so far this year. Rocket Lab moved within one flight of Electron’s 100th launch on Monday, deploying iQPS’s WADATSUMI-II radar-imaging satellite. “The Sea God Surveys” marked its 20th mission of 2026 and tenth successful iQPS launch, with eight more dedicated missions booked through 2030. The launch momentum supported Citizens’ bullish stance. The firm reiterated ‘Market Outperform’ and a $90 target, viewing Neutron’s delay as a timing setback and expecting its debut in late fiscal second-quarter 2027. However, its broader expansion is still under scrutiny. title: Nvidia Stock To $129? - Trefis
content: Part of our AI selloff guide. Start here: what the Nasdaq correction means for your money. Follow the whole story: every piece in this series is on our AI storyline page. The Nasdaq 100 closed Monday more than 10% below its Oct 6 peak, which is the textbook definition of a correction. The worst day was Friday, Oct 30, when chip stocks (the iShares Semiconductor ETF) fell about 8% after Amazon’s and Alphabet’s results and a weak profit forecast from Intel. By Wednesday the index had bounced to about 9% below its peak, but chip stocks fell another 3% that day. The fear behind the selloff is simple: JPMorgan expects about $900 billion of AI spending worldwide in 2026, and investors want to know when that money pays back. The stock at the center of AI spending is down the least. The deepest falls are company-specific or come after the biggest run-ups. If this were purely a vote against AI spending, Nvidia, the biggest chip company and the one most tied to that spending, should be leading the way down. It isn’t. Intel lost more than a third of its value in five days after its own forecast. Micron and Dell are down hard, but both had more than doubled over the past year. 12-month price changes to Nov 4: Micron +265%, Dell +141%, AMD +95%, Marvell +82%, Intel +57%, Nvidia +1%, Broadcom −8%, Super Micro −38%. Prices are the Wed Nov 4 close (Trefis market data). AMD closed Tue Nov 3, before its report, at $483.90. “Below 52-week high” is how far each stock sits under its highest close of the past year. A stock that more than doubled can fall 30% and still be up on the year; Micron is the clearest case. Company-specific. Intel fell on its own weak profit forecast, not on anyone’s AI budget. Its 39% five-day drop is the biggest in the table. Super Micro has been falling for a year (−38% over 12 months) for reasons that started before this selloff. The payoff doubt. Memory (Micron), networking and optical chips (Marvell) and the companies that build AI servers (Dell, Super Micro) all sold off together after the big cloud companies reported. These businesses get paid first when data centers are built, so they’re the first to be marked down when investors worry that building slows. Marvell’s 36% five-day drop is the biggest of that group. Nvidia and Broadcom sit in between. They are the biggest chip companies selling into AI spending, but they’ve held up best over the past five days (−7% each). That tells you the market isn’t yet betting that the spending stops. It’s betting that the spending gets more careful, and that the suppliers with the thinnest edge get squeezed first. A lot further than this, usually. From late 2021 to late 2022, chip stocks (the iShares Semiconductor ETF) fell about 46% from their peak, and Nvidia fell about 66%. In late 2018, Nvidia lost more than half its value in about three months. In the 2000–2002 bust, many chip stocks fell by more than 80%: Intel about 82%, AMD about 93%. And it’s not only chips: Meta fell about 77% from its 2021 peak to its 2022 low, and it stayed profitable throughout. Here’s what a 2022-sized fall (46% from the 52-week high) would mean for each stock today: The 52-week highs are each stock’s highest close of the past year. For Nvidia, a repeat of its own 2022 fall (−66%) would mean about $81 a share. That’s the outer edge, not a forecast. In 2022, the Fed was raising interest rates fast, from near zero to above 4%. That isn’t the main story today. Here’s what this table means at home: if you own broad index funds, you own every one of these stocks, often on top of the ones you bought yourself. Chip stocks have fallen 46% to 66% before, in less than a year. If you have $1 million or more invested, a Trefis partner firm can show you how much of your portfolio rides on one industry. That the slowdown investors fear hasn’t reached AMD’s order book. It reported after the close on Tuesday, Nov 3: third-quarter revenue of $13.4 billion, up 45%, against about $13.1 billion expected, and record data center revenue of $8.5 billion, up 97%. The number that mattered was the fourth-quarter guide: about $17 billion, plus or minus 3%, against the roughly $16.3 billion analysts expected. CEO Lisa Su added that she expects revenue to grow more than 80% in 2027. AMD closed Tuesday at $483.90, before the report, 25% below its 52-week high. After rising more than 4% in early trading Wednesday, it closed up only 1.0%, at $488.78, while Nvidia fell 3.2%. The market took it as good news for AMD, not yet as an all-clear for the group: AMD can grow by taking share even if total AI spending slows, and Nvidia, already far bigger than AMD, has less room to do that. What AMD’s guidance says about the slide, and whether the drop was overdone. Nvidia reports on Tuesday, Nov 17. It guided this quarter’s revenue to about $108 billion, plus or minus 2%. Nvidia is the real test of the payoff question because its customers are the companies doing much of that $900 billion of spending. If its outlook for next quarter keeps rising, the selloff in suppliers looks like a scare. If it flattens, the 2022 yardstick starts to apply to Nvidia too. Two of the eight have already fallen as far as chip stocks did in 2022; Nvidia has fallen about a third of that far. The worst drops of the past five days are Intel’s own forecast and a reset in the suppliers that had run furthest. AMD’s beat-and-raise on Tuesday says its customers are still buying; whether the whole group avoids a 2022-style reset now rides on Nvidia’s report in about two weeks.
